claims.text: The protective coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure.
The as-deposited coating has well-defined FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
The as-deposited coating has minimal pre-existing plastic deformation.
Continuous constant stress at elevated temperature will induce creep conditions in the coating.
The density and distribution of FCC/BCC phase boundaries govern the coating's creep resistance.
FCC/BCC phase boundaries obstruct dislocation motion during sustained high-temperature loading.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by phase boundaries delays the accumulation of plastic strain.
Delayed plastic-strain accumulation enhances creep resistance relative to a single-phase microstructure.
The dual-phase coating will accumulate less creep strain than the single-phase baseline under the specified test conditions.
The dual-phase coating will show a smaller increase in dislocation density than the single-phase baseline.
The phase-boundary mechanism is expected to dominate under sustained high-temperature and high-stress conditions.
At lower temperatures or stresses, phase boundaries may have less influence on creep resistance.
Additional microstructural factors and processing variations may affect creep resistance.
A comparison at approximately 600 °C and 100 MPa for 500 hours can test the proposed mechanism.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant creep-strain reduction in the dual-phase coating would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe lower dislocation density in the dual-phase coating would falsify the hypothesis.
